before_after.before: We evaluate automation based on whether it reduces the overall effort required on the part of the shopper. Accurate notifications about product availability on the shelf are only useful if someone responds to them. Fast checkout loses its value if it becomes difficult to correct an error on the receipt. Therefore, in this diagram, intelligent systems are linked to specific staff responsibilities.
before_after.after: We evaluate automation by whether it reduces shoppers' overall effort. Accurate shelf alerts are only useful if someone responds. Fast checkout is less useful if correcting a receipt error becomes difficult. The blueprint therefore links intelligent systems to specific staff responsibilities.

before_after.before: Wirtz et al. (2018) distinguish between routine work tasks and situations requiring emotional and social judgment. Their conceptual model supports the automation of repetitive checks while retaining staff to resolve contentious situations. However, their conceptual predictions do not confirm the system’s acceptance by local consumers. Similarly, the company’s publications describe initiatives rather than independent satisfaction tests. Carrefour in the UAE should test task performance and the level of effort required by consumers before expanding the proposed system.
before_after.after: Wirtz et al. (2018) distinguish routine service tasks from situations requiring emotional and social judgment. Their framework supports automating repeated checks while retaining staff for disputes. These conceptual predictions do not establish local customer acceptance. Company publications also describe initiatives rather than independent satisfaction tests. Carrefour UAE should test task performance and customer effort before expanding the proposed system.

before_after.before: Employees can save time through automated checks, but they are faced with a large number of alerts, the need for monitoring, and complex exceptional situations involving customers. Carrefour should involve sales floor staff in developing alerts, organize paid training, and evaluate both workload and response times. An unresolved alert should not automatically be considered a sign of poor employee performance in the event of a stockout. Managers remain responsible for personnel decisions and corrective actions; the use of third-party software does not shift this responsibility to customers. For the company, integration and maintenance costs may exceed the savings if alerts are inaccurate. A limited pilot project allows for service continuity while simultaneously testing this risk.
before_after.after: Employees may save time through automated checks while facing more alerts, monitoring, and difficult customer cases. Carrefour should involve shelf staff in alert design, provide paid training, and measure workload alongside response times. An unresolved alert should not count as poor employee performance when stock is unavailable. Managers remain responsible for staffing and recovery; using third-party software does not remove their responsibility to customers. Integration and maintenance costs may exceed savings if alerts are inaccurate. A limited pilot protects service continuity while testing this risk.

before_after.before: Carrefour UAE combines the sale of traditional food products with services that help customers find, compare, and pay for them. Majid Al Futtaim manages the business in the UAE. Its ESG report notes that in 2021, the number of Tally inventory robots was increased in 11 additional Carrefour stores in the UAE (Majid Al Futtaim, 2022, p. 44). This provides a basis for studying the use of robots in these stores, although it does not mean that they are currently present in every store. Figure 1 presents a simplified diagram of customer interactions in a typical traditional grocery store from planning what to put in the shopping cart to resolving post-purchase issues.
before_after.after: Carrefour UAE combines tangible groceries with services that help customers find, compare, and pay for them. Majid Al Futtaim manages the UAE business. Its ESG report records the expansion of Tally inventory robots to 11 additional UAE Carrefour stores during 2021 (Majid Al Futtaim, 2022, p. 44). This supports studying robots in these stores, although it does not establish their presence in every store today. Figure 1 proposes an improved service blueprint for a typical physical grocery store, from planning a basket to resolving post-purchase issues.

before_after.before: Huang and Rust (2021) distinguish between “mechanical AI” for repetitive tasks, “thinking AI” for analytical decision-making, and “feeling AI” for interpreting interactions and emotions. If we apply this classification to Figure 1, the repetitive scanning of shelves falls primarily into the first category; recognizing missing items and recommending alternatives require analytical processing. These capabilities can coexist within a single system. A friendly greeting alone does not indicate an understanding of emotions. A barcode scanner is a self-service technology, but not necessarily AI. In this scenario, the intelligence lies in interpreting images of the shelves and product requests; the checkout counter remains the interface for payment. We should not attribute to AI benefits that are already provided by conventional automation.
before_after.after: Huang and Rust (2021) distinguish mechanical AI for repetitive tasks, thinking AI for analytical decisions, and feeling AI for interpreting interactions and emotions. In Figure 1, repetitive shelf scanning falls primarily into the first category; recognizing missing items and recommending alternatives require analytical processing. These capabilities can coexist within one system. A friendly greeting alone does not indicate emotional understanding. A barcode scanner is self-service technology, but not necessarily AI. Here, intelligence lies in interpreting shelf images and product requests; checkout remains the payment interface. We should not attribute to AI benefits already provided by conventional automation.

before_after.before: Tally is a physical robot: it moves through the aisles and collects information about the products on the shelves. A report by Majid Al Futtaim describes checks for missing, misplaced, and incorrectly priced items. A chatbot is software that processes information; it cannot restock the shelves. In Stage 3, the proposed link between the robot’s signal and the employee’s restocking task resolves Problem F2, where the recorded product availability differs from what a customer can actually purchase. This is a service reliability issue, despite the physical nature of the products. Restocking remains a human task, and staff must verify ambiguous signals.
before_after.after: Tally is a physical robot: it moves through aisles and collects shelf information. Majid Al Futtaim's report describes checks for missing, misplaced, and incorrectly priced items. A chatbot processes information; it cannot restock shelves. At stage 3, the proposed link between a robot alert and an employee's restocking task addresses fail point F2, where recorded availability differs from what a customer can buy. This is a service reliability issue, despite the physical nature of the products. Restocking remains a human task, and staff must verify uncertain alerts.

before_after.before: Carrefour has also tested software tools outside the UAE. In June 2023, Carrefour announced the Hopla service on its French website, which offers shopping recommendations tailored to users’ budgets and dietary restrictions (Carrefour, 2023). In Brazil, a June 2021 announcement of the Nutri Choice service described an algorithm that compares nutritional values and prices, with recommendations based on purchase history (Carrefour, 2021). None of these announcements confirm the service’s launch in the UAE. They mention an optional planning assistant offered in Phase 1 and product comparisons in Phase 4. Recommendations must use data from the local catalog and show the rationale behind them; nutritional ratings cannot replace checking ingredients.
before_after.after: Carrefour has also tested software tools outside the UAE. In June 2023, it announced Hopla on its French website, offering shopping recommendations based on budgets and dietary restrictions (Carrefour, 2023). Brazil's June 2021 Nutri Choice announcement described an algorithm comparing nutritional scores and prices, with recommendations based on purchase history (Carrefour, 2021). Neither announcement confirms a UAE deployment. These examples inform our proposed optional planning assistant at stage 1 and product comparisons at stage 4. Recommendations must use local catalog data and explain their basis; nutritional ratings cannot replace checking ingredients.

before_after.before: Visualizing the purchasing journey changes our perception of quality service. In Stage 1, shoppers may appreciate recommendations that fit their specified budget, while continuing to check package sizes and current prices. Figure F1 illustrates how persuasive recommendations can create expectations that a store may not be able to meet. Displaying the source of information and the time it was last updated would help shoppers assess the degree of uncertainty before they even visit the store. We believe that a clear warning about uncertainty regarding product availability is more helpful than a confident promise.
before_after.after: Visualizing the purchasing journey changes our perception of quality service. At stage 1, shoppers may appreciate recommendations within their budget while still checking package sizes and current prices. Fail point F1 shows how persuasive advice can create expectations the store cannot meet. Displaying the source and update time would help shoppers assess uncertainty before visiting. We believe a clear warning about uncertain availability is more helpful than a confident promise.

before_after.before: When entering a store and searching for products, aisle signs and convenient routes continue to play an important role, even when using digital aids. The approach described in the course—treating customers as “partners”—explains why delegating tasks to shoppers can reduce labor costs while simultaneously increasing the workload for customers (Wirtz, 2023) . A search screen would be useful if it saved time spent moving around, except in cases where entering information takes longer than asking an employee for help. Therefore, in Stage 2, the route is maintained without using the app. The physical service environment and the digital interface should support the same customer journey.
before_after.after: When entering a store and searching for products, aisle signs and accessible routes remain important even with digital aids. The course's treatment of customers as co-producers explains why transferring tasks to shoppers can reduce labor costs while increasing customer work (Wirtz, 2023). A search screen would help if it saved walking, unless registration took longer than asking an employee. Stage 2 therefore keeps a route without an app. The physical servicescape and digital interface should support the same journey.

before_after.before: At F2, we believe that a stocked shelf is more important than having a robot. If you follow the arrows in Figure 1, it becomes clear that the following steps must occur before the stock status changes: detection, verification by staff, and restocking. Scanning alone cannot deliver the promised benefits. It is worth mentioning the “line of sight” principle here: shoppers rely on work that is typically performed out of their field of vision.
before_after.after: At F2, we believe a stocked shelf is more important than having a robot. Following the arrows in Figure 1 shows that detection, staff verification, and restocking must happen before the availability message changes. Scanning alone cannot deliver the promised benefits. The line of visibility helps explain this: shoppers depend on work usually performed out of their sight.

before_after.before: In Stage 4, another question arises: Who controls the choice? The shopper may well reject an option that meets the target price but conflicts with their dietary preferences. An explanation of the recommendation and an offer of assistance from staff during Stage F3 would support such a choice. At the checkout stage, self-checkout also places the responsibility on the shopper to scan items and verify the total amount. The absence of a discount at stage F4 should prompt a price check, and the shopping cart should be saved so the shopper does not have to start over.
before_after.after: At stage 4, who controls the choice? A shopper may reject an option that meets the target price but conflicts with their dietary preferences. Explaining the recommendation and offering staff assistance at F3 would support that choice. Self-checkout also makes shoppers responsible for scanning items and verifying the total. A missing discount at F4 should prompt a price check, with the basket saved so the shopper does not have to restart.

before_after.before: After a purchase, we will evaluate the seller based, among other things, on how easily they correct mistakes. At F5, having to re-enter the same data first into a chatbot and then to a staff member would create unnecessary work. Forwarding the request record to an authorized colleague would avoid the need to ask the customer to start over from the beginning. This aligns with the principle of process redesign covered in the course: eliminating unnecessary steps and ensuring the ability to recover in the event of a self-service failure (Wirtz, 2023). We will seek reliable assistance throughout the entire interaction, especially when something goes wrong.
before_after.after: After purchase, we would evaluate the retailer partly by how easily it corrects mistakes. At F5, repeating the same details to a chatbot and then a staff member would create unnecessary work. Forwarding the case record to an authorized colleague would avoid asking the customer to start again. This applies the course's process-redesign principle: remove unnecessary steps and provide recovery when self-service fails (Wirtz, 2023). We would seek reliable assistance throughout the interaction, especially when something goes wrong.

before_after.before: Personalization creates a conflict between useful recommendations and excessive data collection. The Brazilian service Nutri Choice demonstrates how purchase history can serve as the basis for recommendations (Carrefour, 2021). In the case of the proposed assistant in the UAE, these records could also reveal confidential dietary preferences. In stages 1 and 4, guest mode should operate without saving the purchase profile. Separate consent for storing preferences and for marketing purposes would allow shoppers to choose convenience without disclosing irrelevant data. A short retention period and restricted access would reduce the risk of information disclosure, although a smaller volume of historical data could weaken personalization.
before_after.after: Personalization creates a conflict between useful recommendations and excessive data collection. Brazil's Nutri Choice shows how purchase history can support recommendations (Carrefour, 2021). For the proposed UAE assistant, these records could also reveal sensitive dietary preferences. At stages 1 and 4, guest mode should work without saving a purchase profile. Separate consent for saved preferences and marketing would let shoppers choose convenience without disclosing unrelated data. Short retention and restricted access would reduce exposure, although less historical data could weaken personalization.

before_after.before: Commercial interests can also influence recommendations. Juan and Rast (2021) warn that optimization can lead to biased results even in the absence of intentionally discriminatory instructions. If the assistant offered by Carrefour prioritizes profit margins, it may become more difficult to find cheaper, suitable products. Retailers should label sponsored offers and provide the option to sort by price per unit. The final choice remains with the shoppers. Advertising revenue should not depend on shoppers mistaking paid advertising for unbiased advice.
before_after.after: Commercial interests can also influence recommendations. Huang and Rust (2021) warn that optimization can produce biased results without intentionally discriminatory instructions. If Carrefour's proposed assistant prioritizes profit margins, cheaper suitable products may become harder to find. The retailer should label sponsored offers and allow sorting by unit price. Shoppers retain the final choice. Advertising revenue should not depend on shoppers mistaking paid placements for unbiased advice.

before_after.before: Physical robotics affects more than just app users. Virtz et al. (2018) highlight privacy and security issues arising from robots’ sensory capabilities. In Phase 3, the analysis of in-store equipment should minimize the recording of customers who can be personally identified, and the use and storage of any accidentally captured images should be restricted. The robot must yield to people and have an accessible stop procedure. In Phase F3, the presence of staff ready to provide assistance and clear instructions protects shoppers with limited confidence in using digital technology, language barriers, or disabilities. Ensuring equal access comes at a cost; however, mandating self-service will shift the retailer’s operational burden onto those who are least able to handle it.
before_after.after: Physical robotics affects more than app users. Wirtz et al. (2018) identify privacy and safety concerns arising from robots' sensing capabilities. At stage 3, shelf analysis should minimize capture of identifiable shoppers, with restricted use and retention of incidental images. The robot must yield to people and have an accessible stop procedure. At F3, staffed assistance and readable instructions protect shoppers with limited digital confidence, language difficulties, or disabilities. Equal access costs money, but compulsory self-service would shift the retailer's operational burden onto those least able to handle it.

before_after.before: The store operations manager and the inventory management team should conduct a pilot implementation of the “notification-to-restocking” process (Phase 3) before implementing additional customer-focused automation tools. Conduct a four-week pilot after establishing baseline metrics, ensuring it includes both peak and off-peak periods. The financial manager should compare the savings in operating expenses against the costs of equipment, maintenance, and training. Expanding operations should ensure higher product availability without increasing the number of complaints or the workload, rather than simply increasing the number of alerts processed. Track alert accuracy, the time to confirmed restocking, and product availability on the shelves compared to the results of manual checks during similar sales periods. The F2 system only completes an operation after staff have checked the shelf. This fail-safe mechanism prevents a situation where an unfinished task results in a false promise of product availability. Monitor blocked aisles and staff workload; suspend robot operations following safety incidents.
before_after.after: The store operations manager and inventory team should pilot the stage 3 alert-to-restocking process before adding more customer-facing automation. Use a four-week pilot after recording a baseline, with matched peak and off-peak periods. The finance manager should compare operating savings with equipment, maintenance, and training costs. Expansion should require better availability without increased complaints or workload, rather than simply more alerts processed. Compare alert accuracy, time to verified shelf correction, and shelf availability against manual checks during comparable trading periods. Close the alert at F2 only after staff verify the shelf. This failure-proofing control prevents unfinished tasks from creating false availability promises. Monitor blocked aisles and staff workload; suspend robot operations after a safety incident.

before_after.before: Teams responsible for digital products and merchandising should test the optional assistant on pages F1 and F3 in comparison with standard product search. Evaluate compliance with budget constraints, the number of unconfirmed recommendations, and task completion, including instances where customers use the option involving staff assistance. Test various language options and accessibility requirements. Ensure consistent offers and service entitlements across all channels. If a recommendation cannot be supported by current catalog data, indicate the uncertainty and offer assistance from a staff member. Avoid implementing personalized ranking until its commercial incentives and data control mechanisms are clear.
before_after.after: The digital product and merchandising teams should test the optional assistant at F1 and F3 against standard product search. Measure budget compliance, unsupported recommendations, and task completion, including customers using staff assistance. Test different language and accessibility needs. Keep the same offers and service entitlements across routes. If current catalog data cannot support advice, show uncertainty and offer staff help. Avoid personalized ranking until its commercial incentives and data controls are clear.

before_after.before: The cashier floor supervisor and the customer service manager should share responsibility for metrics F4 and F5. It is necessary to consolidate information about the product, price, and receipt into a single file, obtain confirmation from the customer before making corrections, and grant employees the authority to act within the agreed-upon refund policy. Proposed pilot standards: acknowledgment of an in-store assistance request within two minutes and a staff member’s response within one business day to post-purchase inquiries. Track the percentage of cases meeting these standards, the number of follow-up inquiries, and the total resolution time; these are proposed targets, not measured outcomes.
before_after.after: The checkout supervisor and customer service manager should jointly own fail points F4 and F5. Transfer item, price, and receipt details into one case, obtain customer confirmation before corrections, and give employees authority within an agreed refund policy. Proposed pilot standards are staff acknowledgment within two minutes of an in-store help request and a human response within one working day for a post-purchase case. Track the share meeting these standards, repeat contacts, and total resolution time; these are proposed targets, not measured outcomes.
